cards.q: A machine is stopped with its emergency stop latched in. Is its wiring safe to work on?
options: Yes: the emergency stop cuts all the power
No: isolate, lock off and prove dead first
Yes, once the motors have stopped turning
Yes, if the stop is latched and taped over
cards.why: An emergency stop works through the control circuit. The supply into the panel stays live, a contactor can weld, and anyone can reset the button.

cards.q: At the point of work there are {n} conductors, earth included. How many tests does proving them dead take?
cards.why: Every conductor against every other, once: $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. Single-phase (L, N, E): 3. Three-phase, no neutral: 6. With neutral: 10.

cards.q: Why is the voltage indicator proved again straight after testing the circuit dead?
options: It may have failed mid-test, and would read dead
The first proof only warms the tester up
It checks the proving unit's own battery
The law asks for two readings of each circuit
cards.why: A broken lead or a blown lead fuse reads exactly like a dead circuit. A good proof afterwards shows the tester was working when it gave those readings.

cards.q: A single-phase load draws {i} A from a 230 V supply. What is its apparent power, in kVA?
cards.why: Apparent power is volts × amps: $S = VI$, in VA; ÷ 1000 for kVA.

cards.q: A load takes {s} kVA at a power factor of {pf}. What real power does it use, in kW?
cards.why: Real power = apparent power × power factor: $P = S \cos\phi$. The rest is reactive power, which flows back and forth without doing work.

cards.q: A three-phase 400 V motor draws {i} A at a power factor of {pf}. What real power does it take, in kW?
cards.why: Three-phase: $P = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \cos\phi$, with the line voltage and line current.

cards.q: A three-phase supply has a line voltage of {vl} V. What is the phase voltage (line to neutral) in star?
cards.why: In star, $V_{phase} = \frac{V_{line}}{\sqrt{3}}$: 400 V between lines is 230 V to neutral.

cards.q: In a delta-connected load, how does the line current compare with the current in each winding?
options: The same as the winding current
A third of the winding current
cards.why: In delta each line feeds two windings, and their currents are 120° apart, so the line current is $\sqrt{3}$ times the phase current. In star the two are equal.

cards.q: A motor would draw {i} A at the moment of starting if connected in delta. About what does it draw starting in star?
cards.why: In star each winding gets $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ of the voltage, so $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ of the winding current, and the line current falls by another $\sqrt{3}$: a third in all (and a third of the torque).

cards.q: A 24 V DC panel supply must deliver {i} A. What power rating is that, at least, in watts?
cards.why: Power = volts × amps: 24 × {i} W. Then allow some spare.

cards.q: A control transformer steps {vp} V down to {vs} V. Its secondary supplies {is2} A. Assuming an ideal transformer, what current does the primary draw?
cards.why: The power in equals the power out: $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$, so $I_p = I_s \times \frac{V_s}{V_p}$. Stepping the voltage down steps the current up.

cards.q: Why does a control transformer's primary often need a slower fuse or a type D breaker?
options: Transformers draw less current when warm
The secondary side is never fused at all
Its switch-on inrush can be many times full load
A faster fuse would overheat the windings
cards.why: Switching on a transformer can draw a large magnetising surge for a few cycles. A fast device sized on full-load current trips on it, though nothing is wrong.

cards.q: On a 50 Hz supply, what is the frequency of the {n}th harmonic, in Hz?
cards.why: A harmonic is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental: {n} × 50 Hz.

cards.q: Which current harmonics does a drive with a six-pulse rectifier mainly draw from the supply?
cards.why: A six-pulse bridge draws harmonics of order 6k ± 1: 5, 7, 11, 13… Chokes, filters or 12-pulse and active front ends reduce them. Triplen (3rd) harmonics come mainly from single-phase loads.

cards.q: A current has a {i1} A fundamental, a {i5} A 5th harmonic and a {i7} A 7th harmonic (and nothing else). What is its total harmonic distortion, in %?
cards.why: THD = the RMS of all the harmonics ÷ the fundamental: $\frac{\sqrt{I_5^2 + I_7^2}}{I_1} \times 100$. Harmonics add as squares, not straight.

cards.q: A type B circuit breaker trips at once (magnetically) at about what multiple of its rated current?
cards.why: BS EN 60898: type B 3–5 × In, type C 5–10 ×, type D 10–20 ×. Type C and D ride through motor and transformer inrush.

cards.q: What does a 30 mA RCD actually measure?
options: The current in the line conductor alone
The voltage between neutral and earth
The temperature of the circuit's cable
The difference between current out and current back
cards.why: If current leaks to earth, for instance through a person, less comes back than went out. A 30 mA RCD trips on that difference. It does not see overloads or line-to-neutral faults: that is the breaker's job.

cards.q: A type C breaker is rated {inom} A. What current is certain to trip it at once (the top of its magnetic band, 10 × In), in A?
cards.why: Type C trips instantly somewhere between 5 and 10 × In. Only 10 × In is sure to, so fault-loop checks use that figure.

cards.q: Two fuses are in series, one feeding the other. For discrimination, what must happen on a fault after the second one?
options: Only the fuse nearest the fault blows
cards.why: Discrimination (selectivity) keeps the rest of the installation running: the upstream fuse is sized larger, with a margin from the makers' tables, so the one nearest the fault clears first.

cards.q: A cable's volt drop is {mv} mV/A/m. It carries {i} A over {l} m. What is the volt drop, in V?
cards.why: BS 7671 method: mV/A/m × amps × metres gives millivolts; ÷ 1000 for volts.

cards.q: A cable is rated {it} A as tabulated. Grouping with others gives a factor of {cg}, and the ambient temperature a factor of {ca}. What current can it carry installed, in A?
cards.why: The correction factors multiply the tabulated rating down.

cards.q: A cable's volt drop is {mv} mV/A/m. It carries {i} A over {l} m on a 230 V circuit. What is the drop as a percentage of 230 V?
cards.why: Volt drop in volts, then ÷ 230 × 100. BS 7671 suggests 3% for lighting and 5% for other uses on a public supply.

cards.q: What must be true of the design current Ib, the protective device's rating In, and the cable's current-carrying capacity Iz?
cards.why: The device must carry the load (In ≥ Ib) and protect the cable (In ≤ Iz). BS 7671 regulation 433.1.1.

cards.q: Match each earthing system with how it is earthed.
pairs: A separate earth from the supplier, often the cable's sheath
Neutral and earth combined in the supply (PEN), split at the origin
Your own earth electrode; the supplier gives no earth
The supply is not earthed, or earthed through a high impedance
cards.why: T: earth (terre); N: connected to the neutral; S: separate; C: combined. TN-C-S is often called PME.

cards.q: The external earth loop impedance Ze is {ze} Ω and the circuit's R1 + R2 is {r} Ω. What is Zs?
cards.why: $Z_s = Z_e + (R_1 + R_2)$: the loop out from the supply and back through the circuit's own conductors.

cards.q: A type B {inom} A breaker trips at once at 5 × In. Using 230 V × 0.95, what is the highest Zs that still trips it at once, in ohms?
cards.why: $Z_s \le \frac{U_0 C_{min}}{I_a}$, with $I_a = 5I_n$ for type B. For B32: $\frac{218.5}{160} \approx 1.37$ Ω, as in BS 7671's tables.

cards.q: Insulation resistance on a 230 V circuit: what test voltage and minimum reading does BS 7671 give?
cards.why: For circuits up to 500 V: test at 500 V DC, minimum 1.0 MΩ. SELV and PELV circuits: 250 V, 0.5 MΩ. Disconnect anything the test voltage could damage.

cards.q: A radial circuit is {l} m of 2.5 mm² line conductor (7.41 mΩ/m) with a 1.5 mm² protective conductor (12.10 mΩ/m). What should R1 + R2 be, in ohms?
cards.why: Add the two per-metre resistances (19.51 mΩ/m), times the length, ÷ 1000 for ohms.

cards.q: Put these tests in the usual order for a new circuit.
cards.why: Dead tests first (continuity, insulation, polarity), so the circuit is known safe before it is energised; then the live tests (earth fault loop impedance, then the RCD).

cards.q: About how much current does an induction motor draw when started direct on line?
options: The same as at full load
cards.why: At standstill there is no back-EMF to hold the current down, so the starting current is several times full load, for a second or two.

cards.q: What does a soft starter do?
options: Runs the motor at any speed you choose
Reverses the motor with no second contactor
Ramps up the voltage to ease the start
Corrects the power factor while running
cards.why: A soft starter eases the start (and sometimes the stop), then runs the motor at full speed, often bypassed. Speed control needs a VFD.

cards.q: A motor's full-load current is {flc} A. Its star-delta starter has the overload in the winding circuit, so it carries phase current. What should it be set to, in A?
cards.why: In delta the winding (phase) current is the line current ÷ $\sqrt{3}$, about 0.58 × FLC.

cards.q: Match each conductor colour in a machine's panel (BS EN 60204-1) with its use.
pairs: Circuits left live when the main isolator is off
cards.why: BS EN 60204-1's recommended colours; the drawings still decide, so check.

cards.q: An enclosure is rated IP54. What do the digits mean?
options: 5 mm and 4 mm holes are allowed
54 V is the highest safe voltage
cards.why: IP (BS EN 60529): the first digit is solid objects and dust, the second water. 5: dust-protected; 4: splashing water from any direction.

cards.q: BS EN 60204-1 requires a supply disconnecting device on a machine. What must it be able to do?
options: Isolate the equipment, and lock in the OFF position
Stop the machine faster than an emergency stop
Switch the control circuits off only
Reset the safety relay after a trip
cards.why: It must isolate the machine's electrical equipment from the supply, have one OFF and one ON position, and be lockable OFF, so people can lock it off for work.

cards.q: Match each gas zone with how often an explosive atmosphere is present.
pairs: Likely now and then in normal operation
Not likely, and only briefly if it happens
cards.why: Dust uses zones 20, 21 and 22 the same way. The zone sets the category of equipment allowed.

cards.q: In Great Britain, which regulations require employers to classify places where explosive atmospheres may occur?
cards.why: The Dangerous Substances and Explosive Atmospheres Regulations 2002 require the risk assessment and zoning. Equipment for those zones must meet the equipment regulations (ATEX/UKEX).

cards.q: Which equipment category may be used in a Zone 1 gas area?
cards.why: Category 1 suits zone 0, 2 zone 1 and 3 zone 2; a higher category may always be used in a lower zone. G is for gas, D for dust.
